title: Mentoring is not a script, a shoulder, or a checklist
author: Dr Haili Hughes
summary: Haili Hughes argues that school-based mentoring of trainee teachers is diminished when it is reduced either to instructional coaching scripts or to pastoral reassurance. She credits instructional coaching with bringing precision to teacher education, but insists a trainee is a novice thinker under heavy cognitive load, not merely a performer learning moves. She proposes four facets mentor training must cover: emotional and motivational support grounded in belonging research, evidence and decision-making, getting better at teaching through small rehearsable steps, and the slow development of teacher expertise. Each facet on its own produces a characteristic failure, from kind conversations that leave practice untouched to tidy coaching with shallow roots. Her conclusion is that mentors need a curriculum rather than a briefing, including practice at moving between comfort and challenge. Mentoring, she argues, should be humane, precise and intellectually serious.
points: Hughes accepts Kraft, Blazar and Hogan's evidence for coaching but argues that trainees also need help with the cognitive overload Sweller's work predicts for novices.
Emotional support is framed as the condition for pursuing standards, not a substitute for them: good mentors name the difficulty, isolate the improvable part and explain why it is learnable.
She warns that coaching can mistake movement for meaning, with a trainee performing cold call or circulation while still missing the learning.
Expertise development means making expert noticing visible, taking mentor meetings 'beneath' the lesson into why a text was hard or which prior knowledge was missing.
Her training prescription: mentors need a curriculum, worked examples of good and weak feedback, and rehearsal of mentor conversations.
quotes: Yet a trainee teacher is not merely a novice performer learning a set of moves. They are a novice thinker in a complex environment.
Mentoring, then, has to do more than polish techniques. It has to reduce unnecessary load, build usable mental models, protect motivation, and connect immediate action to longer-term expertise.
This is not softness. It is not sympathy in place of standards. It is the condition which allows standards to be pursued without the trainee shutting down.

Trainees experience belonging uncertainty too. They may enter the staffroom unsure how to speak, unsure whether questions make them appear weak, unsure whether one poor lesson proves they should leave.
But coaching weakens when it mistakes movement for meaning. A trainee can perform a routine without understanding the problem it solves.

If we train mentors only in instructional coaching, we risk producing tidy development conversations with shallow roots. If we train them only in care, we risk kind conversations which leave practice untouched.
It is the professional education of a novice teacher in a live school, among real pupils, under pressure. It should be humane. It should be precise.
